findings.description: AWS access key and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is readable by anyone with instance metadata access or console/API permission to describe the instance, leading to credential leakage.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the management interface of the instance to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.

The security group allows inbound TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no TLS listener defined anywhere in the configuration, exposing an unencrypted web service directly to the internet; combined with the public subnet and auto-assigned public IP, this materially widens the attack surface.

The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true (the setting is explicitly commented out), leaving data at rest on the block device unencrypted and readable if the underlying storage or a snapshot of it is exposed.

The snapshot is taken from the unencrypted source volume and has no encryption configured, so a persisted copy of the disk contents remains unencrypted, increasing exposure if the snapshot is shared or made public.

map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing any instance launched in this subnet (including web_host, which sits behind a security group open on SSH and HTTP) to automatically receive a public IP and become directly internet reachable.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, meaning any instance placed in this subnet is automatically assigned a public IP, expanding the network's public attack surface unnecessarily.
The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration, leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

No public access block, bucket policy, or ACL restrictions are defined for the flow logs bucket, leaving it reliant on account-level defaults and susceptible to misconfiguration that could allow public read/write access.
